lede: Hike odds fall to 47%; the 10-year still matches its 2007 high; PCE today.
geo_headlines: OCTOBER HIKE ODDS FELL FROM 70% TO 47% IN ONE SESSION. FedWatch now shows a 46.5% chance of an October 28 hike, down from 69.8%; a December hike is still 91.0% priced. New York Fed President Williams: "there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," though one more hike "may be appropriate late this year" (CNBC). Barr took the other side, saying further increases are likely needed.

THE LONG END DID NOT GET THE MEMO. Treasury's curve: the 2-year fell 3bp to 4.89% on the softer Fed path, but the 10-year rose 2bp to 5.26%, matching its June 12, 2007 close, and the 30-year rose 3bp to 5.59%. **The 2s10s curve steepened to 37bp: less Fed, more term premium.** The 30-year touched about 5.62% intraday, its highest since 2002 (Reuters).

CONSUMERS ARE GLOOMIER THAN THE ECONOMY. Conference Board confidence fell 6.7 points to 81.9, the lowest since 2014, against expectations of about 89 (CNBC). Job openings were little changed at 7.1 million in August (BLS). Reuters' framing: nominal growth near 8-9% and 4.1% unemployment, yet Americans are the most insecure about jobs in more than five years.

OIL FELL 2.5% TUESDAY ON SUPPLY, STEADY THIS MORNING. The Energy Department offered up to 40 million barrels of SPR loans, and Goldman estimates Gulf exports are back to their 2025 average (investingLive). The November Brent contract expires today at about $103; the active December contract is $97.65 (+1.6%) and WTI $90.74 (+1.5%). Trump again denied offering Iran sanctions relief; Qatar says it is still working toward common ground (Reuters).

STOCKS SLIPPED; CHIPS AND CRUISES ROSE. S&P 500 -0.17% to 7,670.84, Dow -132 points; the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.21% and semis 1.31%. Carnival jumped 13% after beating and raising guidance; Apple fell 2.7%. The S&P is 1.64% below its August 13 record and the Nasdaq 100 1.28% below its September 22 record. VIX 16.04.

ASIA RALLIED ON CHIPS; EUROPE OPENED HIGHER. The Nikkei was up about 2.1% in the afternoon, with SoftBank up more than 6% (AP); the ASX gained 1.1%. China's official manufacturing PMI returned to 50.1. Australian CPI was 4.0% but core was softer than forecast. The FTSE opened up 0.8% and the DAX 0.7% (QNA). S&P futures flat; Nasdaq futures -0.09%.

TODAY IS THE BIG ONE: PCE, GDP, THEN MICRON. August PCE prices at 8:30 AM are expected up 0.3% on the month and 3.7% from a year ago (Dow Jones via CNBC), alongside the Q2 GDP third estimate and ADP at 8:15. Governor Cook speaks at 3:25 PM and Micron reports after the close. It is also quarter-end, which Reuters flags as a source of volatility.
client_frame_short: The Fed story got a little softer yesterday, and the bond story did not. Traders cut the odds of an October rate hike from about 70% to under 50% after a senior Fed official said there is no rush. **But long-term Treasury yields still rose, so borrowing costs for mortgages and businesses are not getting relief from a gentler Fed.** Stocks barely moved, and chip stocks rose. Today's inflation report is the real test; nothing here calls for action before we see it, and yields near 5% remain an opportunity for idle cash.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, there are two headlines that seem to conflict, and explaining why they do not is the useful part.

First, the Fed. On Monday markets saw about a 70% chance of another rate hike in October. By Tuesday afternoon it was under 50%. New York Fed President Williams said there is no urgency and the Fed has time to gather data, and consumer confidence dropped to its lowest since 2014. A softer path for the Fed pulled the 2-year Treasury yield down. Job openings were steady at 7.1 million, so this is not a labor market cracking; it is a Fed signaling patience after already hiking in September.

Second, long rates. The 10-year Treasury still rose to 5.26%, matching its June 2007 close, and the 30-year reached levels last seen in 2002. That is investors demanding more to lend for a long time: large deficits, sticky inflation and heavy borrowing to fund AI data centers. Mortgage and corporate borrowing costs key off these long rates, so relief from the Fed is not reaching them.

We said a 10-year close above 5.25% would change our view. It closed at 5.26%, so it is worth being precise about what changes. It raises the bar for rate-sensitive stocks and real estate, and it strengthens the case for locking in longer bond yields for clients who need income, since those yields are the best on offer in almost two decades. It does not change the equity plan: the S&P 500 is 1.64% below its August 13 record, and stocks fell less than 0.2% on the day, with semiconductors up more than 1%. Diversified portfolios built for a higher-rate world are doing their job.

The next test is this morning's PCE inflation report, expected at 3.7% year over year. What would change the view further: a hot PCE print that pushes October odds back above 70%, a 10-year close above 5.40%, or the 30-year holding above 5.75%.
